definitions.explanation: The biological order Rodentia, comprising mammals such as mice, rats, squirrels, beavers, and porcupines that share continuously growing front incisors used for gnawing. Used both as a technical zoological term and in everyday writing about animals.

examples.japanese: {鼠|ねずみ}は{齧歯類|げっしるい}だ。
リスや{兎|うさぎ}も{齧歯類|げっしるい}に{含|ふく}まれると{思|おも}われがちだ。
examples.english: Squirrels and rabbits are often mistakenly thought to be included among rodents.

examples.japanese: {齧歯類|げっしるい}は{哺乳類|ほにゅうるい}の{中|なか}で{最|もっと}も{種類|しゅるい}が{多|おお}い。
examples.english: Rodents are the most species-rich group within mammals.

examples.japanese: {齧歯類|げっしるい}の{前歯|まえば}は{一生|いっしょう}{伸|の}び{続|つづ}けるため、{常|つね}に{何|なに}かを{齧|かじ}って{削|けず}らなければならない。
examples.english: Because rodents' incisors grow continuously throughout their lives, they must constantly gnaw on something to wear them down.

notes:
Composed of {齧|げっ} (to gnaw), {歯|し} (tooth), and the suffix {類|るい} (kind; class; -idae). Literally 'the gnawing-tooth class,' the name highlights the defining trait of the order — a single pair of continuously growing incisors in each jaw.

USAGE:
A biological category term, used in science writing, nature documentaries, veterinary contexts, and pet-shop literature. Like other {〜類|るい} group names ({哺乳類|ほにゅうるい} mammals, {爬虫類|はちゅうるい} reptiles), it sounds technical but is fully comprehensible to general readers. Note that rabbits ({兎|うさぎ}) are NOT rodents — they belong to the order Lagomorpha ({兎形目|うさぎがたもく} or ウサギ{目|もく}) — though many laypeople assume otherwise.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {齧歯類|げっしるい}に{属|ぞく}する: to belong to the rodents
- {齧歯類|げっしるい}の{動物|どうぶつ}: rodent animals
- {小型|こがた}の{齧歯類|げっしるい}: small rodents
- {齧歯|げっし}{目|もく}: order Rodentia (formal taxonomic term)

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {哺乳類|ほにゅうるい}: mammals — the broader class to which rodents belong
- {鼠|ねずみ}: mouse; rat — the most familiar example of a rodent
- {兎形目|うさぎがたもく}: order Lagomorpha — the order containing rabbits and hares (often confused with rodents)
- {爬虫類|はちゅうるい}: reptiles — a parallel taxonomic group of similar formality
